sources.news_title: Billionaires aren’t off the hook for higher taxes, even if they did dodge California’s wealth tax
California voters reject billionaire wealth tax proposal
sources.text:
California voters reject billionaire wealth tax proposal
Opponents spend over $333m against Proposition 40, splitting Democrats
Voters in the state of California rejected a ballot measure that would have taxed the wealth of billionaire residents, a first in the US, according to a projection by the Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).
About 54% of voters opposed Proposition 40 and 46% backed it, with 76% of ballots counted as of 8:51pm EST (0151GMT Saturday).
The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth, with most revenue going to state healthcare programs and the rest to food assistance and education.
The state Democratic Party, the American Federation of Labor, the Congress of Industrial Organisations and the Teamsters unions supported the measure, while California Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed it.
The term-limited governor said he supports a federal billionaire tax but criticised the plan for directing "almost all of the revenue" to healthcare.

"There is nothing for housing, nothing for childcare, nothing for public safety workers who must answer 911 calls, and nothing for our public universities that have powered California’s economy for a decade," he wrote in a Substack post in June.
Billionaires, including many Silicon Valley executives, gave more than $333 million to the nonprofit Building a Better California to oppose the measure.
The state’s Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated a tax on about 200 billionaires would have raised tens of billions of dollars.

sources.news_title: California Billionaire Tax Falls After Opponents Spend More Than $300 Million
sources.text:
SACRAMENTO, CALIFORNIA — California voters have rejected Proposition 40, the closely watched measure that would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on residents worth more than $1 billion, according to a projection from Decision Desk HQ.
With roughly three-quarters of ballots counted, about 54% opposed the measure and 46% supported it. The Associated Press had not yet called the race Friday, but Proposition 40 had consistently trailed by a substantial margin.
The proposal would have applied to roughly 250 California billionaires and generated tens of billions of dollars, according to state estimates. Ninety percent of the revenue would have gone toward healthcare, with the remainder funding food assistance and education programs.
Opponents dramatically outspent supporters. Billionaires and business groups poured more than $300 million into efforts opposing Proposition 40 and promoting competing measures that could have blocked it. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone contributed more than $100 million.
Gov. Gavin Newsom also opposed the measure, arguing it could encourage wealthy residents to leave California and destabilize state revenues. Supporters, including Sen. Bernie Sanders and the California Democratic Party, argued billionaires should contribute more toward healthcare and social programs.
The defeat does not necessarily end the wealth-tax debate. Democratic leaders nationally have already indicated that taxing extremely wealthy Americans will remain part of their agenda.

sources.news_title: California rejects billionaire tax proposal in win for executives, Newsom
Voters in Silicon Valley rejected the billionaire wealth tax while those in Los Angeles and San Francisco—home to the two top AI companies—wanted it
sources.text:
California is still counting the votes for the 2026 election, but the controversial billionaire wealth tax looks headed for defeat—with help from Silicon Valley.
Statewide, the “no” side for Proposition 40 is getting 55% of the vote versus 45% voting “yes.” That split exactly matches how it played out in Santa Clara County, home to tech strongholds like Sunnyvale, Palo Alto, Cupertino, and Mountain View.
The wealthy Bay Area enclave of Marin County, which sits just north of San Francisco, also came out against Prop 40 as did San Mateo County, which is just south of the city.
By contrast, 55% of San Francisco County voters were in favor of Prop 40 and 45% were against. That’s despite being home to top AI startups OpenAI and Anthropic, which are planning to go public soon and will create new millionaires—and billionaires.
Of course, plenty of employees and early investors in the AI giants live outside San Francisco and likely voted according to their pocketbooks as Prop 40 sought a one-time 5% tax on billionaires.
Opponents of the ballot measure warned it was unlikely to remain a one-time levy, and the way it would’ve taxed privately held assets raised fears founders might have to sell controlling stakes in their companies.
That concern may have resonated especially across the startups and venture capital firms in Silicon Valley who are not quite billionaires yet but have aspirations to become one.
Fearing the possibility of a wealth tax, several billionaires have already fled California, including Google cofounder Sergey Brin, who helped finance the campaign to defeat Prop 40.
And because the state already relies heavily on the wealthy for its budget, it doesn’t take much to move the needle, which perhaps weighed on voters’ minds as well.
The loss of just six billionaires drastically reduced estimates of how much the wealth tax would’ve raised in revenue while also cutting forecasts for how much revenue California could generate from income taxes in the future.
Meanwhile, the election results revealed another split within the state. Los Angeles County voters were in favor of Prop 40, 53% versus 47%.
Unlike Northern California, which is a tech hub that’s leading the AI charge, Southern California is an entertainment hub that’s threatened by AI-generated content.
Alongside the campaign against Prop 40, opponents also pushed competing ballot measures designed to nullify the proposed billionaire wealth tax.
One of them is leading in the vote tally. Prop 42 would prohibit taxes on personal savings, assets and retirement holdings.
It dovetailed with a key anti-Prop 40 message, namely that the billionaire tax could someday be expanded to includes everyone else’s wealth, too.
But Prop 40’s defeat and Prop 42’s ban on future wealth taxes doesn’t mean the issue is going away forever. In fact, even some of the opponents of the billionaire tax were against it because it was restricted to one state and not a nationwide levy that would be harder to dodge.
“A ‘no’ vote doesn’t mean similar measures won’t ever be implemented,” Michael Feispor, partner on EY’s private tax team, said in a statement. “Taxpayers who have been watching from the sidelines should use this window to revisit their residency, domicile, and estate planning structures—because now they have some more time to plan.”
He added that wealthy Californians are already asking hard questions about residency, with some acting on them.
For those who remain in the state, methods for organizing wealth that avoid steep estate taxes, such as irrevocable trusts, are becoming more important.
“The question isn’t whether this kind of tax or something similar comes back—it’s whether taxpayers are prepared when it does,” Feispor said. “Whatever the outcome, this tax debate isn’t over and has elevated the importance of long-term planning for individuals and families.”

sources.news_title: California’s wealth tax didn’t catch the blue wave
‘What a waste’: How California’s billionaire tax campaign fell apart
Billionaire tax results show that Californians worry squeezing the ultra-rich would harm the economy
sources.text:
Billionaire tax continues to trail as many Californians vote to spare the state’s ultra-rich stars
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires to help fund healthcare, appeared headed for defeat, though votes were still being counted.
- Opponents raised hundreds of millions of dollars to fight the measure, far outspending supporters, who argued the tax could help offset federal healthcare cuts.
- The campaign also faced opposition from Gov. Gavin Newsom, teachers, business groups and others, while voters weighed concerns about taxing assets and the possibility that billionaires could leave California.
Despite a nationwide blue wave in the midterm election, the much-debated billionaire tax didn’t get the support many expected in one of the country’s most liberal states.
Since the state’s powerful healthcare union proposed the new tax, supporters of Proposition 40 have faced a fierce, expensive battle against the world’s richest people. In what has been described as a David-versus-Goliath fight, the underdog appears to have lost.
The proposition, which would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, seemed headed toward defeat as votes continued to be tallied Saturday.
How each county in California voted for the billionaires tax Proposition 40 and its two counter ballot measures, Proposition 41 and 42.
“In a deep blue state like California, most voters are going to support additional funding for healthcare, especially to replace Trump funding cuts,” said Dan Schnur, a politics and communications professor at USC, UC Berkeley and Pepperdine. “But in retrospect, the sponsors may wish they’ve been a little bit less ambitious.”
As of the public tally on Saturday, around 54% of California voters rejected the proposal while 46% voted yes on Proposition 40. While support for the proposition has edged up slightly in the latest results, it still looked like a long shot, with more than 70% of votes counted.
The $293 million spent by California billionaires to oppose Proposition 40 is about 0.07% of their estimated wealth.
Officials still needed to count more of the votes before they could declare final results.
Although more than half of voters in some urban counties, including Los Angeles and San Francisco, backed the billionaire tax proposal, it lost in the vast majority of counties statewide. In Orange County, the vote against the tax led by more than 20%.
The battle over the billionaire tax has been one of the most expensive ballot-measure fights in California’s history, sparking a debate over wealth inequality and taxing the ultra-wealthy. It also highlighted how billionaires have wielded more influence in politics.
Proposition 40 would affect hundreds of billionaires. Foes have funded two measures that could stymie 40 even if it passes.
Well-known politicians such as U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), the California Democratic Party, healthcare workers and Hollywood celebrities including actor Mark Ruffalo, backed the wealth tax. But the idea drew opposition from California Gov. Gavin Newsom, the teachers union, Planned Parenthood, business groups and others who expressed fears that billionaires could flee the state.
The state’s next governor, Xavier Becerra, also opposed the tax.
Though California’s $4.25-trillion economy remains a global powerhouse and a major draw for investments in AI and aerospace, thousands of businesses have moved to Texas and other states in recent years due to lower costs.
Campaigns supporting and opposing the billionaire tax proposal are paying social media influencers, some with millions of followers, to post videos to inform and sway voters.
Opponents of the wealth tax heavily outspent Proposition 40 supporters, flooding televisions, radio, social media and smartphones with ads. Their message: the wealth tax is a reckless experiment and a tax on everyone, not just billionaires.
UC Berkeley law professor Brian Galle, who helped write the wealth tax proposal, said it’s tough to “fix a broken system” and get the facts to people when they were up against the ultrawealthy. Billionaires also own media outlets and social media companies, megaphones that help spread political messaging.
“When billionaires have half a dozen different strategies for buying this election, it shows that they already have too much money and pay too little back,” he said.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West President Dave Regan denied the allegations. He said he did not attempt to extort from union officials, or assault or threaten female labor leaders.
Support for the billionaire-bashing proposition had waned in recent months.
A poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies, co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times and released last week, showed voter support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 42% from 52% in March.
The measure also may have lost fans because taxing assets rather than income can be a complicated and confusing process. It sparked concerns among even non-billionaires about whether they want to let the state start demanding a slice of the value of what they own. No matter the result, Proposition 40 also fueled a conversation about taxing billionaires that will continue beyond the election, Galle said.
Hundreds of millions of dollars were raised to support and oppose Proposition 40 along with two ballot measures — Propositions 41 and 42 — that could block the wealth tax, data from the California secretary of state show.
Money doesn’t always win an election, but a big funding imbalance is tough to overcome, Schnur said.
“As important as the money was to beat Prop. 40, the coalition against it may have been just as important. You didn’t see Sergey. You didn’t see tech billionaires in the ads. You saw teachers and nurses and firefighters,” he said.
The four richest Californians —Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang; Google co-founder Larry Page and Meta Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg — would owe 40% of the estimated taxes to be collected from the billionaire tax, according to an L.A. Times analysis.
The billionaire tax proposal also faced other big hurdles. Proposition 42, which could have blocked the billionaire tax, was also on track to pass. It would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” and bar retroactive taxes.
“They didn’t just reject a single bad tax idea — millions of Californians backed the strongest protections available to protect their hard earned life savings from double taxation. They joined firefighters, law enforcement officers, building trades workers, seniors, veterans and small businesses in doing so,” said Nathan Click, a spokesman for Proposition 42.
Supporters of Proposition 40 tried to convince voters that taxing roughly 200 billionaires would raise the $100 billion needed to offset federal healthcare cuts.
This week, the wealth tax’s supporters emphasized the high stakes. People won’t be able to afford healthcare coverage, children will die and hospitals will shutter, they said, if California lawmakers don’t find a way to get more funding.
“If Sacramento fails to protect patients and deliver a real solution that makes billionaires pay their fair share, healthcare workers will pursue every available avenue, up to and including returning to the ballot in 2028 with a billionaire tax,” said Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for the SEIU-UHW.

sources.news_title: Update: What we know about results in all 14 California ballot propositions
sources.text:
BY ADAM ECHELMAN
CalMatters
Voters decided the fate of 14 statewide propositions this week, including the contentious billionaire tax. The campaigns for and against these propositions have spent a total of nearly $1 billion — the most in history on state ballot measures.
Beyond the billionaire tax, Californians faced decisions on a wide range of topics, including how recall elections are conducted, speeding development by capping environmental reviews, and whether the state should put more money toward housing and medical research.
Below are the early results:
Prop. 1: This measure authorizes the state to borrow up to $11.25 billion toward housing construction and renovations, mostly for rental units. Many developers and local governments that receive the money would have to reserve a portion of it for affordable housing for low-income renters or for specialized housing that serves the homeless.
The measure passed, with 60.5% of voters in favor of the bond as of Friday.
Prop. 2: Voters decided to allow the state to deposit more money into its reserves, otherwise known as the rainy day fund. California has a fairly volatile tax system that rises and falls with the incomes of its highest earners, but 1970s-era state rules limit how much money the state can save in surplus years.
The measure passed with 60.8% of voters supporting it as of Friday.
Prop. 3: This income tax for high earners would send more money to K-12 education. First passed in 2012 as a temporary measure, this tax, which affects individuals making over $360,000 a year, would become permanent if voters approve Prop. 3.
The measure passed, with 59.9% of voters in favor as of Friday.
Prop. 4: This measure would allow the state and local governments to create public financing for political campaigns, which proponents say could help cap political spending. In order to accept public money for campaigns, candidates usually have to accept certain spending limits.
No is leading, with nearly 50.9% of voters opposed as of Friday.
Prop. 5: California’s recall elections ask voters whether they want to oust the officeholder and who they want instead. This measure would make it so that recall elections only ask whether voters want to remove the elected official from office. A second election would determine who should replace the officeholder.
Bottom of Form
Yes is leading, with a slim margin as of Friday.
Prop. 37: The state would create a new fund that gives out loans to middle-class homebuyers if Prop. 37 passes. Homebuyers who benefit from the fund would slowly pay back the state.
The measure passed with more than 61% of voters supporting it as of Friday.
Prop. 38: This measure would pump $8.4 billion in state funding to immunology research — with a catch: About half the money would go to one, three-person nonprofit organization, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. Gary K. Michelson, the institute’s co-founder, put this proposition on the ballot.
Yes is leading, with 54.7% of voters in favor as of Friday.
Prop. 39: This ballot proposition would increase identification requirements for California voters. This campaign, funded in large part by Illinois billionaire Richard Uihlein, would require state voters to provide proof of citizenship at the polls or write their Social Security number or other government-issued ID number on mail-in ballots.
The measure will fail with more than 60% of voters opposing it as of Friday.
Prop. 40: The contentious billionaire tax would enact a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth. The healthcare workers union that put the measure on the ballot says it would raise roughly $100 billion over five years and help struggling healthcare programs. Opponents point out that billionaires pay a large share of state taxes already and worry it could cause them to flee the state.
No is leading, with 53.9% of voters opposed as of Friday.
Prop. 41: Created by the opponents to the billionaire tax, this measure would invalidate Prop. 40 by creating stricter rules about new California taxes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass, whichever gets more votes will prevail.
No is leading, with 54% of voters opposed as of Friday.
Prop. 42: Also created by the opponents to the billionaire tax, Prop. 42 would make it harder for the state to levy a new tax on wealth, such as investment accounts or personal property, and effectively invalidate the billionaire tax. If voters approve both Prop. 40 and Prop. 42, the measure with the most votes will win.
Yes is leading, with 52.6% of voters in favor as of Friday.
Prop. 43: This measure would make it harder for local citizen-driven tax measures to pass. These local tax measures only need a majority to win, but if Prop. 43 passes, they would need two-thirds of the vote.
No is leading, with more than 56% of voters opposed as of Friday.
Prop. 44: Health clinics would need to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on patient care if Prop. 44 passes. The measure is backed by the same union that proposed the billionaire tax, Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West.
The measure will fail with 82% of voters opposing it as of Friday.
Prop. 45: Voters will decide whether to pare down California’s landmark environmental review law, known as CEQA. The 1970 law requires agencies to consider environmental harm before building, but developers say the law is often a tool to delay much-needed affordable housing and infrastructure projects.
No was leading, with more than 55% of voters opposed as of Friday.
